newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - World seen heading for 2nd bumper wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - World seen heading for 2nd bumper wheat crop.

text.p: World wheat production is set to jump again in 1997, even after 1996's bumper crop, according to a leading monitoring organisation.
The London-based International Grains Council on Thursday released new estimates showing the world's grains crop at 585 million tonnes in 1997, compared with 580 million in 1996.
These two good years follow a drought hit 541 million tonnes produced in 1995.

In 1997, production is set to rise in Russia and Ukraine, as well as across Europe as the European Union eases limits on the area farmers can plant and countries further east recover from a poor 1996, the IGC said.
But Argentina, Canada and Australia, three of the world's biggest exporters, are expected to see falls as they return to more normal levels after excellent 1996 crops.

The grain market is now calmer after a dramatic "spike" in prices about a year ago on supply fears and on news that world stocks were at the lowest in two decades following drought in Russia and elsewhere.

Low stocks prompted fears that world food security was under threat. Low stocks were seized upon by opponents of EU production cuts which slashed the infamous grain mountains built up by Europe in the 1980s.
Now bellwether Chicago wheat futures are trading just below $3.75 per bushel compared with a record $7.50 hit last March.
China too is slated to see a fall in its wheat crop, after a bumper 1996, which has meant Chinese imports lower than international traders hoped.
Thursday's IGC report cut its forecast of imports by China for 1996/97 to 5.0 million tonnes from a previous estimate of 7.0 million. A year earlier, China imported 12.6 million tonnes.
Lower imports by the Chinese may also help take the heat out of the grains market and ease pressure on cash-pinched Third World importers.
One country the IGC expects to import more is Iraq, due to benefit from the UN oil-for-food deal.

The IGC has revised its estimate for Iraq's 1996/97 wheat imports up to 1.8 million tonnes, from a previous estimate of one million. But the IGC concedes that "operational procedures governing the lifting of the UN embargoes on trade with Iraq are not yet complete."

The deal, finally implemented in December, allows Iraq oil sales of $2 billion in six months to buy food and medicine for its more than 20 million people suffering from trade sanctions imposed by the United Nations after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
